content: People with diabetes mellitus are at a higher risk of experiencing complications after surgery. Evidence from randomized clinical trials and meta-analyses suggests that intensive glycaemic control, aiming for near-normal blood glucose levels, may benefit individuals with hyperglycaemia, regardless of whether they have diabetes. However, there is limited evidence specifically addressing the effects of intensive glycaemic control in people with diabetes undergoing surgery. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of perioperative glycaemic control in people with diabetes undergoing surgical procedures. To achieve this, databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, LILACS, WHO ICTRP, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to July 25, 2022, without language restrictions. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intensive glycaemic control to conventional or standard care in diabetic patients were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two authors. Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality, hypoglycaemic events, and infectious complications. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular events, renal failure, length of hospital and ICU stay, health-related quality of life, socioeconomic effects, weight gain, and mean blood glucose levels during the intervention. Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model, and the certainty of evidence (CoE) was assessed using the GRADE approach. This update included 20 RCTs, with eight new studies added to the 12 from the previous review. A total of 2670 participants were randomized, with 1320 in the intensive glycaemic control group and 1350 in the conventional care group. The duration of interventions ranged from the intraoperative period to five days postoperatively. None of the included trials had an overall low risk of bias. Intensive glycaemic control showed little to no difference in all-cause mortality compared to conventional glycaemic control (10.3% vs. 9.1%; risk ratio [RR] 1.08, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.88 to 1.33; high CoE). However, hypoglycaemic events, both severe and non-severe, were more frequent in the intensive glycaemic control group. Intensive glycaemic control may slightly increase the risk of hypoglycaemic events (11.9% vs. 3.3%; RR 3.36, 95% CI 1.69 to 6.67; low CoE) and severe hypoglycaemic events (4.0% vs. 0.6%; RR 4.73, 95% CI 2.12 to 10.55; low CoE). Regarding infectious complications, intensive glycaemic control may result in little to no difference compared to conventional glycaemic control (13.0% vs. 18.2%; RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.04; low CoE). For cardiovascular events, intensive glycaemic control may reduce the risk compared to conventional care (11.2% vs. 12.7%; RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.97; low CoE). There was little to no difference in renal failure events between the two groups (13.3% vs. 14.9%; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.22; low CoE). The length of ICU stay (mean difference [MD] -0.10 days, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.38; low CoE) and hospital stay (MD -0.79 days, 95% CI -1.79 to 0.21; very low CoE) showed little to no difference between the two groups. Mean blood glucose levels were reduced in the intensive glycaemic control group, with reductions ranging from 13.42 mg/dL to 91.30 mg/dL, but data were not pooled due to variability among studies. One trial assessed health-related quality of life using the SF-12 survey and found no significant differences between the groups. A cost analysis from one substudy indicated higher total hospital costs in the conventional glycaemic control group compared to the intensive glycaemic control group. It is important to note significant heterogeneity among studies in terms of clinical outcomes and methodological approaches. Two ongoing trials may provide additional insights in future updates. In conclusion, high-certainty evidence suggests that intensive perioperative glycaemic control does not reduce all-cause mortality in people with diabetes undergoing surgery compared to conventional glycaemic control. Low-certainty evidence indicates that intensive glycaemic control may reduce cardiovascular events but has little to no effect on infectious complications and may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. There is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about other outcomes, such as health-related quality of life, socioeconomic effects, and weight gain. Further high-quality studies are needed to address these uncertainties and improve the evidence base, particularly for outcomes like hypoglycaemia and infectious complications.
